title: Boil water to make it safe
summary: Boiling is the most reliable way to kill disease germs in water when the supply is unsafe.
how_it_works: Filter cloudy water through a clean cloth first. Bring clear water to a rolling boil for 1 minute (3 minutes at altitudes above ~2,000 m / 6,500 ft), then let it cool and store covered.
caveat: Kills germs but does NOT remove chemical contamination, fuel or heavy metals.

title: Disinfect water with household bleach (CDC)
summary: Plain unscented household bleach makes water safe to drink when you can't boil.
how_it_works: Use unscented household bleach (5–9% sodium hypochlorite). Add 2 drops per litre/quart, 8 drops per gallon (a bit less than 1/8 teaspoon), or 40 drops (1/2 teaspoon) per 5 gallons. Stir and let stand at least 30 minutes — the water should have a slight chlorine smell. Double the dose if the water is cloudy, coloured or very cold.
caveat: Measure exactly; bleach must be unscented and fresh. Over-chlorination is unsafe. Not a substitute for a safe utility supply.

title: Bleach dosing by concentration (EPA)
summary: If your bleach states its strength, dose by concentration for accuracy.
how_it_works: Per 1 gallon of water: 8 drops of 6% bleach, OR 6 drops of 8.25% bleach. Stir and let stand 30 minutes; if there is no slight chlorine odour, repeat the dose and wait another 15 minutes. Double the dose for cloudy or cold water.
caveat: EPA figures assume 6% / 8.25% US bleach. If your bottle differs, use the CDC 5–9% method instead.

title: SODIS — disinfect water with sunlight
summary: Clear water in a plastic bottle left in strong sun becomes safe to drink — no fuel, no chemicals.
how_it_works: Fill clear, colourless PET plastic bottles of 1–2 litres (water no deeper than ~10 cm) with low-turbidity, clear water. Lay them on their side in direct sun for at least 6 hours under bright to partly cloudy sky; if it is fully overcast, leave them out across 2 consecutive days.
caveat: Only works on clear water — pre-filter turbid water. Does not remove chemical contamination.

title: Pre-filter cloudy water before disinfecting
summary: Remove dirt and particles first so disinfection actually works.
how_it_works: Pour cloudy water through a clean cloth, paper towel or coffee filter to remove sediment before boiling, chlorinating or using SODIS. Ceramic/membrane filters need a pore size of about 1 micron or less to remove parasites and 0.3 micron for bacteria — and they still will not remove viruses, so follow filtration with chemical disinfection.
caveat: Filtration alone is not enough for viruses — always disinfect after filtering.

title: Make a chlorine stock from pool granules (fallback)
summary: When no liquid bleach is left, calcium hypochlorite granules can be made into a disinfecting stock.
how_it_works: In a ventilated area, wearing eye protection, dissolve about 1 heaping teaspoon (~1/4 oz) of granular calcium hypochlorite (HTH) in 2 gallons of water to make a stock solution (~500 mg/L). Then disinfect drinking water by mixing 1 part of this stock into 100 parts water (about 1 pint of stock per 12.5 gallons).
caveat: HTH is a strong oxidant — handle and store strictly per label; not for inexperienced users; never mix with other chemicals.

title: Store treated water safely
summary: Treated water stays safe only in clean, covered containers.
how_it_works: Store boiled or treated water in clean, sanitized containers with tight covers. Sanitize containers before filling, keep them off the floor, and rotate self-stored water regularly. Replace sealed commercial water by its date.
caveat: Re-contamination is common — never dip dirty hands or cups into stored water; pour instead.

title: Plan around minimum water quantities
summary: Know how much water per person per day to aim for so you ration realistically.
how_it_works: Humanitarian planning uses about 15 litres per person per day as the basic survival standard (drinking, cooking and hygiene combined). In acute scarcity, 7.5 litres per person per day may be tolerable for a short time, but never treat 15 litres as a maximum to aim below.
caveat: These are survival minimums, not targets for normal life; prioritise drinking water for the sick, infants and pregnant people.

title: Oral rehydration solution — home recipe
summary: A salt-and-sugar drink that treats the dehydration from diarrhoea, the biggest killer after services fail.
how_it_works: Only if packaged ORS is unavailable: wash hands, then in a clean container mix 1 litre of safe water + half a level small (teaspoon) measure of salt (3.5 g) + 8 small spoons / 4 big spoons of sugar (40 g). Stir until dissolved. Give frequent small sips.
caveat: Packaged WHO/UNICEF ORS sachets are safer and preferred. Do NOT exceed the salt. Seek care urgently for infants, severe dehydration, blood in the stool, or if there is no improvement.

title: Use packaged WHO/UNICEF ORS when you can
summary: Prepackaged low-osmolarity ORS sachets are the safest first choice for rehydration.
how_it_works: Dissolve one sachet in exactly 1 litre of clean water. The WHO/UNICEF standard formula per litre is 2.6 g sodium chloride, 13.5 g anhydrous glucose, 1.5 g potassium chloride and 2.9 g trisodium citrate (245 mOsm/L). Stock sachets in the household kit before a crisis.
caveat: These are manufacturer quantities for reference/procurement — do not try to weigh them at home; buy sachets.

title: Keep insulin and vaccines cold without grid power
summary: An insulated cool box with conditioned ice packs protects temperature-sensitive medicine through a blackout.
how_it_works: A closed fridge holds safe temperatures for only a few hours. Move temperature-sensitive medicines into an insulated cool box with conditioned ice packs or gel bricks (can hold cold roughly 48 hours) and watch a thermometer. Target 2–8 °C; insulin must not freeze and degrades above about 25–30 °C, so never place vials directly against ice.
caveat: Check each product's labelled temperatures; if the cold chain is broken, ask a clinician before using or discarding.

title: Hand hygiene to stop disease spreading
summary: Washing hands with soap is the single highest-impact act when sanitation breaks down.
how_it_works: Wash hands with soap and safe water at key moments — after defecation, after cleaning a child, and before handling or eating food. Where water is very scarce, use an alcohol-based hand rub. A simple tippy-tap (a hung jug tipped by a foot lever) makes a little water go a long way.

title: Contain excreta when sewerage fails
summary: Keeping human waste away from water and food prevents deadly outbreaks.
how_it_works: When toilets stop working, use a covered bucket or bag latrine, or dig a simple pit sited well away from and downhill of any water source. Cover waste after each use, and wash hands afterwards. Dispose of contained waste safely away from living and water areas.
caveat: Site latrines at least the recommended distance from wells and water; protect children's contact with waste.

title: Manage greywater so it doesn't make you sick
summary: Used washing and cooking water must not pool near homes or reach drinking water.
how_it_works: Keep used washing and cooking water from pooling near dwellings, where it breeds mosquitoes, and out of any drinking-water source. Reuse it for flushing or cleaning, and drain the rest to a simple soak pit.
caveat: Do not reuse greywater on food crops without proper treatment.

title: Lighting and small power through blackouts
summary: Keep lights, phones and medical devices running with batteries, an inverter or solar.
how_it_works: Bridge outages with LED lamps, USB power banks, a 12 V battery plus an inverter, or a small solar panel with a charge controller. Prioritise the loads that matter — light, phone charging, a medical device — and size the battery and inverter to those loads.
caveat: NEVER run a fuel generator indoors or in an enclosed space — carbon monoxide kills.

title: Cook when there's no gas or power
summary: Fuel-efficient and solar cookers let you keep cooking and boiling water off-grid.
how_it_works: Use a fuel-efficient improved cookstove, a charcoal or wood rocket stove, or a solar cooker where the sun is strong. The same fire also boils water for disinfection. Always ventilate to avoid smoke and carbon-monoxide build-up.
caveat: Never burn charcoal or fuel indoors without ventilation.

title: Keep food safe without refrigeration
summary: Eat, preserve, or protect perishable food before it spoils when the fridge is off.
how_it_works: When the fridge is down, eat the most perishable food first, and preserve the rest by drying, salting, fermenting, or cooking and eating it the same day. Keep the fridge and freezer doors closed to hold cold as long as possible; freezing bottles of water in advance buys extra hours.
caveat: When in doubt, throw it out — discard perishable food kept above 4 °C for more than 2 hours.

title: Keep phones and contact alive
summary: Stretch battery and agree how to reach each other before networks get congested.
how_it_works: Lower screen brightness, switch to airplane mode between check-ins, and share power banks. Pre-download offline maps. Agree a family check-in protocol and a single out-of-area contact everyone messages, since local lines clog first.

title: Off-grid mesh messaging (Meshtastic)
summary: Low-cost radios pass encrypted texts with no cell network or internet.
how_it_works: Meshtastic uses inexpensive long-range LoRa radios that form a peer-to-peer mesh, relaying encrypted text messages between devices with no cell network or internet. Range is typically several kilometres, more with an elevated antenna.
caveat: Requires hardware and setup acquired BEFORE the crisis — stage it in advance.

title: Phone-to-phone messaging when networks fail (Briar)
summary: An app that connects phones directly over Bluetooth or Wi-Fi during outages.
how_it_works: Briar is an Android app that connects phones directly over Bluetooth or Wi-Fi (and via Tor when the internet is available), so messaging keeps working during network outages or shutdowns. Install it and add your contacts before you need it.
caveat: Bluetooth range is short (tens of metres); set up contacts in advance.

title: Crowdsourced needs mapping (Ushahidi)
summary: Collect incident and needs reports onto a live map to direct help.
how_it_works: Ushahidi is open-source software that crowdsources incident and needs reports — by SMS or web — onto a live map, so a community or responders can see where water, medicine or rescue is needed and direct mutual aid.

title: Open base maps for response (HOT)
summary: Volunteers trace buildings and roads so responders have usable maps.
how_it_works: The Humanitarian OpenStreetMap Team coordinates volunteers to trace buildings, roads and infrastructure from satellite imagery, producing free, open maps of affected areas that neighbourhood groups and responders can actually use.

title: Neighbourhood mutual-aid committee
summary: An organised block keeps everyone alive through prolonged degraded services.
how_it_works: Stand up a block or building committee: keep a roster of vulnerable residents, set up a shared water and phone-charging point, run a message board, and agree simple signals. This community backbone is what carries people through weeks of degraded services.

title: Check a building before re-entering after a quake
summary: Quick triage of structural and gas hazards before you go back inside.
how_it_works: Before re-entering after an earthquake, check for a gas smell, leaning walls, large cracks, and sagging floors or ceilings. If you suspect a gas leak, shut off the gas — and do NOT switch electrics on or off if you smell gas. Stay out of any visibly damaged structure until it is inspected.
caveat: This is triage only — real structural safety needs a qualified inspector.

title: 3D-printed umbilical cord clamp
summary: A printable clamp that seals a newborn's umbilical cord to prevent infection.
how_it_works: It replaces the commercial plastic cord clamp that hospitals run out of after a disaster, when staff improvise with shoelaces or glove fingers. Printed from a single piece of filament on any desktop FDM printer, it snaps shut over the cord to stop bleeding and reduce sepsis risk in the first minutes of life.
caveat: Clinical device for skilled birth attendants; print in a clean material and follow sterilisation/aseptic practice before use on a newborn.

title: Oxygen supply fitting
summary: An adapter that connects oxygen tubing to standard oxygen systems.
how_it_works: When a clinic's oxygen delivery fails for want of a small proprietary connector, this printed adapter bridges supply tubing to standard oxygen equipment. It is a 3D-printed part that lets existing cylinders, concentrators and tubing keep working instead of sitting idle.
caveat: Oxygen-delivery component; verify fit, leak-tightness and material compatibility with a clinician before patient use.

title: Oropharyngeal airway (OPA)
summary: A printable airway device that keeps an unconscious patient's airway open.
how_it_works: An OPA holds the tongue clear of the throat so an unresponsive patient can keep breathing — a basic emergency-care item that stockpiles run short of after mass-casualty events. It is printed to standard airway sizing on a desktop printer, giving responders a locally made supply when imported stock is gone.
caveat: Airway-management device; for use by trained personnel only, with correct sizing and a biocompatible, properly finished material.

title: Otoscope specula
summary: Printable ear specula for examining the ear canal and eardrum.
how_it_works: Otoscope tips are disposable and quickly run out in field clinics, halting basic ear exams. These specula print cheaply in batches on a desktop printer and clip onto an otoscope so a clinician can keep inspecting the external canal and eardrum.
caveat: Patient-contact part; clean and disinfect appropriately between patients and use a suitable material.

title: Syphon handwash station
summary: A foot-operated portable handwashing unit built from a simple bucket syphon.
how_it_works: After a disaster, hands-free handwashing slows disease spread but plumbed sinks are rare. This unit turns an ordinary bucket into a foot-operated syphon: 3D-printed parts plus a bucket let people wash without touching a tap, and it can be deployed anywhere water can be carried.

title: Foot-operated tap
summary: A hands-free tap that fits under an existing sink and screws into the plumbing.
how_it_works: It retrofits an ordinary sink for hands-free use, cutting contamination at the tap during outbreaks and water-scarce conditions. The 3D-printed unit sits under the sink and screws into existing plumbing, so a foot pedal controls the flow instead of hands on a handle.

title: Water pipe T-piece
summary: A printable T-junction that joins three flexible pipes.
how_it_works: Repairing or branching a water line stalls when a single fitting is missing and none can be bought. This T-piece prints on a desktop printer and joins three flexible pipes (silicone or PVC, 4-7 mm inner diameter), letting communities mend and extend water and tubing runs locally.
